newsitem.title: THAILAND: Delayed rains seen hitting Thai corn, sugar.
newsitem.headline: Delayed rains seen hitting Thai corn, sugar.

text.p: Dry weather is wreaking havoc in Thailand on top of the country's worst economic slump in over a decade, farm industry sources said on Tuesday.
They said the Thailand's corn and sugar cane production was certain to be hit hard by the late arrival of the rainy season.
Despite improved rainfall recently, the first corn crop in many areas had already been damaged by the lack of rain during the crucial tasseling stage of growth in May and June, they told Reuters.
The recent rains have eased concerns over the possibility of the El Nino phenomenon, which raises sea temperatures off South America and can affect weather all around the world.
Insufficient rains during the sugar cane planting period had also affected the quality of the crop and was likely to result in a 10-15 percent drop in 1997/98 output, the sources said.
Thailand suffered a dry spell between late April and June, and the rainy season normally starts in May.
Industry sources said that domestic corn supplies were now likely to be available only in late August or September and not July as earlier anticipated.

More than 70 percent of the first crop was damaged, according to trade and farm industry sources. Farmers started planting their first corn crop in April and the crop normally enters the tasseling period by June.
The hardest hit areas were in traditional northeastern bread baskets such as Nakorn Rachasima, Prachin Buri, Petchaboon and Sa Kaew provinces, said the sources.
"Corn farmers realised the damage and already started sowing the new crop in June. It will take around 120 days before the crop can be harvested," said an agriculture ministry official.

The Thai Feedmill Association, in anticipation of the shortage, recently requested an additional 100,000 tonnes of tariff-free corn imports on top of the 200,000 tonnes already granted by the government to the industry.

However, an official at Thai Maize and Produce Traders' Association told Reuters that supplies were likely to be delayed. Yet the overall output of the whole crop year was likely to meet the forecast target of 4.53 million tonnes.

"The supplies will be a bit late, no doubt. But farmers who enjoyed good corn prices will make up for the damage and sow more. We don't anticipate any shortages," said Somlak Tomratanarueporn, the association's assistant manager.
Sugar cane production is also likely to be affected, especially in the central and northern regions.

Surat Abhikleophand, head of marketing at the semi-official Thai Cane and Sugar Corp Ltd, told Reuters that based on farmers' estimates, sugar cane output for the 1997/98 crushing season starting in November would be only about 49.123 million tonnes compared with an estimated 56.2 million tonnes for 1996/97.
A long dry spell and massive pre-harvest burning during the 1996/97 season would result in a 10-15 percent drop in production in 1997/98, he added.
"Dry and damaged soil as a result of pre-harvest burning was exacerbated by the lack of rain during the period that is crucial for development of the cane quality," he said.
Only 10-20 percent of sugar cane acreage in Thailand is irrigated; the rest depend entirely on rains.
Rice and tapioca were hardly affected. Farmers in some areas delayed planting rice during May and June but the damage was expected to be minimal.

"Most farmers started growing rice in July. Some might have started early but most of them delayed planting until late June to wait for rain," said Charnchai Tuambamroong, head of the meteorological centre in the northeastern Thai rice bowl.
"With the amount of rainfalls improving in many areas from this week I don't see any trouble for rice," he added.
